latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable gonococci colonize urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal mucosa. The mucosal infection can be minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic when DGI appears.
Gonococcal epithelial invasion and neutrophilic mucosal inflammation produce dysuria, discharge, cervicitis, PID, pharyngitis, or no recognizable symptoms while organisms remain transmissible.
Strain-specific PorB/LOS properties and host complement vulnerability allow organisms to survive serum killing and raise probability of bloodstream dissemination.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Transient gonococcal bacteremia and tissue seeding
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Gonococci enter blood intermittently and seed synovium, tendon sheaths, skin microvasculature, and rarely endocardium, meninges, liver capsule, bone, or other deep sites.

Disseminated gonococcal antigen and host immune response drive migratory polyarthralgia, tendon-sheath inflammation, acral pustular or petechial lesions, and sterile or culture-negative inflammatory fluid.
A viable gonococcal burden in a joint space produces an asymmetric purulent arthritis phenotype with effusion, synovitis, pain with motion, and possible need for drainage.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory response to disseminated gonococci
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bloodstream spread and immune activation produce fever, chills, malaise, leukocytosis, CRP/ESR elevation, and occasionally sepsis physiology.
Sustained dissemination can rarely cause endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, liver abscess, myositis, or severe sepsis; these events dominate mortality when present.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Antimicrobial non-activity, resistance, or delayed therapy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Delayed parenteral gonococcal-active therapy, reduced cephalosporin susceptibility, unrecognized allergy constraints, or undertreatment of deep foci sustains viable burden and complication risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mucosal colonization can produce local urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal inflammation but can remain clinically silent.
DGI starts when organisms disseminate from a mucosal site into blood.
Serum-resistant strains and impaired terminal complement killing make bloodstream survival more likely.
Blood cultures can be positive during bacteremic DGI but are often insensitive.
Disseminated antigen and viable organism exposure trigger the classic arthritis-dermatitis syndrome.
Some DGI presentations localize as true purulent gonococcal septic arthritis.
Bacteremia and disseminated inflammation can produce fever, chills, leukocytosis, and acute-phase reactants.
Persistent dissemination can seed valves, meninges, bone, liver, or muscle, although this is uncommon.
Delayed or inactive therapy sustains viable organism burden and dissemination.
Migratory arthralgia is a core manifestation of the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome.
DGI often inflames wrist, hand, ankle, or foot tendon sheaths.
Acral pustules, petechiae, purpura, or necrotic papules are characteristic but not universal.
Immune inflammatory joint symptoms can be present before or without purulent arthritis.
Purulent arthritis produces an objectively inflamed joint.
Capsular inflammation and effusion cause severe joint pain.
Effusion and periarticular edema produce swelling.
Passive and active motion worsen pain in septic arthritis.
Purulent arthritis often creates an effusion that can be aspirated or washed out.
Purulent gonococcal arthritis or tendon-sheath infection can produce high neutrophilic fluid counts.
Fever is common, although isolated purulent arthritis can be afebrile.
Fever, pain, and inflammation raise heart rate.
Neutrophilic systemic response often causes leukocytosis.
IL-6 driven acute-phase response raises CRP.
ESR rises with sustained inflammation and can remain elevated after symptoms start improving.
Local mucosal gonorrhea may cause dysuria, discharge, or cervicitis, but absence does not exclude DGI.
Pharyngeal gonorrhea can be asymptomatic or present as sore throat before DGI.
Gonococcal endocarditis is rare but carries high morbidity and can require prolonged therapy or surgery.
DGI can rarely involve the CNS and requires longer parenteral therapy.
Bone infection is an uncommon DGI complication, usually near involved joints or tendon sheaths.
Most DGI is not shock-dominant, but severe bacteremia or endocarditis can cause sepsis physiology.
Shock is the main short-term pathway from DGI to death when it occurs.
Endocarditis increases mortality through heart failure, emboli, and persistent bacteremia.
CNS infection raises mortality and neurologic morbidity.
Joint destruction is primarily a morbidity outcome; mortality effect is indirect unless infection remains uncontrolled.

axes.shape_free_text: Fever is common in arthritis-dermatitis DGI but can be absent in isolated purulent arthritis or after antipyretics.
Tachycardia reflects fever, pain, anxiety, or uncommon sepsis physiology.
Usually normal to mildly elevated; higher values suggest sepsis, pain, pregnancy, pneumonia, or another process.
Usually preserved in uncomplicated DGI; hypotension suggests severe sepsis, endocarditis, dehydration, or another source.
Often mild to moderate leukocytosis, but normal values can occur.
Neutrophil predominance supports acute bacterial inflammation but is not specific.
CRP commonly rises in DGI and is especially high in purulent arthritis or delayed presentation.
ESR is often elevated and can lag behind symptom improvement.
Constitutional malaise often accompanies bacteremic DGI.
Myalgias may accompany fever and disseminated inflammation.
Migratory asymmetric pain across wrists, fingers, ankles, knees, elbows, or feet is typical of arthritis-dermatitis DGI.
General arthritis activity can be inflammatory arthralgia or true synovitis; DGI often has asymmetric oligoarticular involvement.
Objectively swollen, warm, tender, or erythematous joint in DGI.
Abrupt painful distal or large-joint involvement, especially wrist, fingers, knee, ankle, elbow, or foot.
Effusion or periarticular edema around involved joints.
Overlying erythema is common for superficial hand or ankle joints but may be absent in deeper joints.
Pain on passive or active joint motion indicates synovitis or purulent arthritis.
Tender, painful, swollen tendon-sheath inflammation, often affecting wrist/hand extensor or flexor tendons or ankle/foot tendons.
Sparse acral pustules, petechiae, purpuric macules, hemorrhagic pustules, or necrotic papules with erythematous rim.
Dusky or necrotic center in a pustule or papule, usually sparse and peripheral/acral.
Dysuria, urethral discharge, cervicitis, pelvic symptoms, or genital inflammation; often absent in DGI.
Sore throat or pharyngitis can precede DGI when oral exposure is involved but is not required.
Recent condomless vaginal, oral, or anal sex raises pretest probability of mucosal gonorrhea and DGI.
Probability that the mucosal source is clinically silent despite DGI.
Blood culture positivity probability for N. gonorrhoeae; useful as confirmatory context but not ordinary presentation evidence.
NAAT positivity from exposed urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal sites; confirmatory/context evidence rather than general ranking evidence.
Synovial or tendon-sheath fluid WBC can be high in purulent arthritis or tenosynovitis; Gram stain/culture may be negative.
Neutrophil predominance in aspirated synovial or tendon-sheath fluid.
Probability of an accessible effusion or purulent collection requiring aspiration, serial drainage, or operative washout.
Ultrasound, CT, MRI, or operative evidence of tendon-sheath fluid, edema, or synovitis.
Need for aspiration, arthrotomy, debridement, tenosynovectomy, or drainage when purulent arthritis or persistent tenosynovitis is present.
Adequacy of drainage or operative source control when a purulent focus exists.
Probability that the selected regimen is active against the infecting gonococcal strain at the involved anatomic site.
Likelihood that the isolate remains susceptible to ceftriaxone; culture and AST are needed for suspected failure or severe disease.
Probability of severe immediate or severe delayed cephalosporin reaction requiring specialist-guided alternative therapy.
Probability of concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis infection or unexcluded chlamydial infection requiring treatment.
Pregnancy changes dissemination risk and antichlamydial choices; doxycycline is avoided.
DGI is usually less shock-dominant than meningococcemia or gram-negative sepsis, but severe bacteremia or endocarditis can progress to shock.
Risk of cartilage destruction, chronic stiffness, or functional loss rises with purulent arthritis and delayed drainage.
Rare but severe endocarditis hazard in DGI.
Rare CNS complication hazard in DGI.
Rare bone infection hazard, often linked to adjacent arthritis or tenosynovitis.
Lifespan outcome hazard for DGI. Mortality is usually low in arthritis-dermatitis or uncomplicated septic arthritis, but rises sharply with endocarditis, meningitis, shock, or delayed active therapy.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both are often driven by the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome mechanism and can co-fluctuate across tendon and joint sites.
Dermatitis and tenosynovitis frequently occur together in classic DGI but either may be absent.
A true inflamed joint, especially purulent arthritis, raises probability of accessible effusion.
Accessible purulent effusion creates a drainage or washout target.
Adequate drainage plus active antibiotics usually allows CRP to fall.
Effective drainage reduces ongoing purulent pressure and cartilage injury risk.
Active parenteral therapy commonly improves fever within days.
Tendon symptoms usually improve after active therapy, though persistent closed-space infection can need washout.
Chlamydia can contribute to mucosal symptoms without explaining the disseminated arthritis-dermatitis syndrome.
Endocarditis can cause persistent bacteremia, heart failure, embolic events, and shock.
Shock is a direct driver of short-term DGI mortality.
Endocarditis is a rare but high-impact DGI complication.
CNS involvement increases mortality and neurologic risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ceftriaxone effect depends on isolate susceptibility and adequate dosing.
Severe cephalosporin reaction can preclude ceftriaxone and requires specialist-guided alternatives.
Endocarditis requires higher-dose/longer parenteral therapy than arthritis-dermatitis syndrome.
CNS involvement requires meningitis-capable parenteral therapy and longer duration.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad-spectrum cephalosporins can rarely precipitate C. difficile colitis.
Mild transient liver enzyme elevation can occur.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral gonococcal-active regimen for arthritis-dermatitis syndrome or gonococcal septic arthritis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Alternative cephalosporins require organism susceptibility and adequate parenteral exposure.
Severe cephalosporin allergy limits this lane.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral cephalosporin lane when ceftriaxone is not used but cephalosporin therapy remains appropriate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oral stepdown is only interpretable when susceptibility and clinical improvement support it.
Oral stepdown is unreliable if a purulent focus remains uncontrolled.
Endocarditis requires prolonged parenteral therapy rather than simple arthritis-dermatitis stepdown.

treatments.context_specific_role: Continuation lane after substantial improvement and susceptibility support, for a total course appropriate to the manifestation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxycycline treats chlamydial coinfection or unexcluded chlamydia but does not by itself treat DGI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Coinfection treatment lane when chlamydia has not been excluded or is confirmed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Azithromycin is used for chlamydia treatment in pregnancy contexts where doxycycline is avoided.
Macrolide add-on is not needed when chlamydia is excluded and there is no other indication.

side_effects.interpretation: Rare QT risk in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Antichlamydial lane when doxycycline is unsuitable or pregnancy context changes the choice.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage can only remove an accessible effusion or purulent collection.
Nonpurulent arthritis-dermatitis syndrome often improves with antibiotics alone.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control lane for purulent gonococcal arthritis or persistent drainable effusion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Closed-space tendon-sheath fluid or persistent inflammation makes washout more useful.
Surgery without active antimicrobial therapy does not clear disseminated gonococcal infection.

side_effects.interpretation: Procedure and immobilization can contribute to stiffness if rehabilitation is inadequate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control lane for persistent or severe tendon-sheath involvement.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises probability of mucosal gonorrhea and DGI; oral exposure can make pharyngeal source plausible.
Historically associated with dissemination risk; pregnancy also changes antimicrobial choices for coinfections.
Raises serum survival, bacteremia, recurrent dissemination, and risk of severe invasive Neisseria infection.
May raise dissemination risk, change inflammatory intensity, and increase complication risk.
Raises probability of gonococcal source and coinfection; chlamydia coinfection changes add-on treatment lane.
Sustains bacteremia, tendon or joint inflammation, and risk of drainage or joint damage.
Shifts phenotype toward source-control need, slower symptom resolution, and joint/tendon morbidity.
Raises antimicrobial failure mechanism, need for culture/AST, public health reporting, and specialist-guided regimen.

supportive_care: Collect NAAT and culture specimens from all exposed urogenital and extragenital mucosal sites and from disseminated sites when feasible, but do not use confirmatory organism identification as ordinary presentation-ranking evidence.
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when this will not delay therapy, recognizing that blood cultures can be negative in DGI.
Aspirate or image an inflamed joint when purulent arthritis is plausible; send cell count, Gram stain, aerobic culture, crystal analysis, and gonococcal NAAT/culture where available.
Evaluate for endocarditis and meningitis when there is murmur, persistent bacteremia, embolic findings, neurologic signs, severe sepsis physiology, or unusually prolonged symptoms.
Screen for HIV, syphilis, chlamydia, pregnancy, and other STI context because coinfections and pregnancy alter care.
Notify and arrange evaluation/treatment of recent sexual partners, with abstinence counseling until patient and partners are treated and symptoms resolve.
Provide analgesia, temporary immobilization or splinting for severe hand/tendon pain, then early range-of-motion therapy after infection control to reduce stiffness.

Consult infectious diseases, orthopedics/hand surgery, or rheumatology when diagnosis is uncertain, purulent effusion exists, symptoms persist despite active therapy, or antimicrobial resistance is suspected.
